title: Israel's Likud Party Picks Its Team for a Super Important Election
summary:
Have you ever had to pick teams for a big game? That's kind of what's happening in Israel right now. The Likud party, which is led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is holding primaries to decide who gets to be on their team for the upcoming election. And this election is a really big deal.

Here's how it works: In Israel, people don't vote for just one person. They vote for a whole party, and that party has a list of candidates. The more votes a party gets, the more people from their list get to be in the Knesset (that's Israel's parliament, like Congress). In the last election, Likud got about 23 percent of the votes, which meant the top 32 people on their list got seats.

But here's the tricky part. Netanyahu gets to personally choose 8 of the top spots on the list, just because he's the leader. He also made deals so 3 other people get spots without having to compete. That means out of the top 30 names, only 15 are actually up for grabs in the primaries. Everyone else is already picked!

Some of the people who already have their spots are pretty controversial. Defense Minister Israel Katz is one of them. He's known for saying really tough things about the war in Gaza. Back in October 2023, he said Israel should cut off water, electricity, and fuel to Gaza until hostages were returned. He also wants to keep Israeli soldiers in southern Lebanon.

Another person with a guaranteed spot is Foreign Minister Gideon Saar. He also has strong opinions about the war and about Israel's critics around the world.

So why does this matter? Well, whoever ends up on Likud's list could become part of the next government. And that government will make big decisions about the war, about peace, and about the future of the region. The primaries are known for being loud and messy, but they're also really important. It's like picking the starting lineup for a game that could change everything.
why_it_matters: When leaders pick their team, it can change big decisions about war and peace, which affect kids' safety and futures around the world.
